Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s petrol supply fell 23 percent in September as imports dwindled and domestic output slipped, leaving fuel stocks short of the regulator’s 30-day safety threshold for a seventh straight month, according to the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority. The country received 38.7 million litres a day of petrol last month, down from 50.5 million in August, the NMDPRA said in its September fact sheet. Diesel receipts dropped 40 percent to 8.7 million litres a day, the lowest in 13 months. The slump comes as fuel remains expensive. Dated Brent crude averaged $116.77 a barrel in September, and the regulator put the naira at N1,327.31 per dollar. The authority’s indicative pump price ranged from N1,369.75 a litre in Ibadan to N1,464.75 in Maiduguri. In Lagos, it was N1,371.01, although the lowest actual prices recorded there were lower. Imports retreat Petrol imports fell 30 percent to 10.2 million litres a day. The NMDPRA said the decline came as approved permit volumes were being exhausted. Domestic refinery supply fell 21 percent to 28.5 million litres a day. Domestic refineries supplied about 74 percent of petrol received, the regulator said, or roughly 65 percent of consumption. That marks a sharp shift from the 13-month average, in which imports made up almost 39 percent of supply. Stock cover remains short Petrol stock cover, which includes inventories at Dangote’s refinery, stood at 23.9 days, up from 22.9 in August but 6.1 days below the 30-day requirement. Cover has risen for four consecutive months, the regulator said, but has not reached the threshold since March, when it was 21.2 days. It peaked at 33 days in January. Diesel cover was far healthier at 49.7 days, and aviation fuel stood at 53.2 days. Cooking gas was the weakest category, with 15.9 days of cover, a deficit of 14.1 days. Demand picked up even as supply fell. Petrol consumption, measured by volumes trucked out into the domestic market, rose 7 percent to 44.4 million litres a day. That is still about 11 percent below the regulator’s 50 million litres benchmark, and below the 13-month average of 50.8 million litres. Dangote runs above nameplate The Dangote refinery ran at 105.98 percent of its 650,000 barrel-a-day capacity in September, the regulator said. It produced 47.22 million litres a day of petrol, of which 28.5 million went to the domestic market, and 15.47 million was exported. Exports made up 35.2 percent of the refinery’s petrol evacuation. Petrol evacuation ran 3.25 million liters a day below production, adding to inventory. Closing petrol stock at the plant was 366.2 million liters. The NMDPRA noted that the refinery’s utilisation implies a crude run of about 689,000 barrels a day against 618,000 barrels received, with the gap drawn from inventory. Crude received by domestic refineries fell 9 percent from August. The state-owned refineries in Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna were not producing. Among smaller modular plants, Duport was shut down, while Aradel and OPAC ran 50 per cent of capacity below because of feedstock problems and maintenance, the regulator said. Those plants together met 4.3 percent of domestic diesel demand. Gas steady, pipelines advance Gas supply, including volumes to Nigeria LNG, slipped 2 percent to 4.822 billion cubic feet a day. Domestic supply fell 6.7 percent to 2.066 billion cubic feet a day. Domestic refineries also supplied about 96 percent of cooking gas received, with total LPG receipts rising 9 percent to 4.7 kilotonnes a day. The Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano gas pipeline was 84 percent complete, down from 88 percent in August after the project was re-scoped to include ancillary facilities, according to the NMDPRA fact sheet.
